title: Definitions
text:
NoteNote



We will list some important equivalent definitions of étale morphisms and leave the discussion of their equivalence for later.

title: Definitions
text:
Equivalent definitions

Definition 1 A morphism \(f\colon X\to Y\) between schemes is étale if it is

locally of finite presentation,
flat, and
unramified.



Definition 2 A morphism \(f\colon X\to Y\) between varieties over \(k\) is étale if it induces isomorphisms on the tangent spaces at all points of \(X\).


Definition 3 A morphism \(f\colon X\to Y\) between schemes is étale if it is smooth of relative dimension \(0\).


Remark 1. The second definition tells us that we can think of an étale map as a map that is locally an isomorphism. And for the definitions of the flat, unramified and smooth morphisms, see later.

title: Definitions
text:
Examples

Example 1 (open immersion) Every open immersion \(U\hookrightarrow X\) is étale. Nothing changes near a point of \(U\): we have only restricted our attention to a smaller open subset.


Example 2 Assume that \(n\) is invertible in the base field. On the punctured affine line, the map
\[
\mathbb G_m \longrightarrow \mathbb G_m, \qquad t\longmapsto t^n
\]
is étale. Infinitesimally, its derivative is \(nt^{n-1}\), which never vanishes on \(\mathbb G_m\).







WarningWhere the picture breaks



On the whole affine line, \(t\mapsto t^n\) ramifies at \(t=0\). The map is no longer étale there: the branches collide.

title: Flat Morphisms
text: Here we study the properties of flat morphisms that we will need as background for étale morphisms.

title: Flat Morphisms
text:
Definitions and basic properties

Definition 1 (flat quasi-coherent sheaf over a base) Let \(\pi\colon X\to Y\) be a morphism of schemes and let \(\mathcal F\) be a quasi-coherent \(\mathcal O_X\)-module. We say that \(\mathcal F\) is flat over \(Y\) at \(x\in X\) if the stalk \(\mathcal F_x\) is flat as an \(\mathcal O_{Y,\pi(x)}\)-module. It is flat over \(Y\) if this holds at every point of \(X\).

On affine opens, this reduces to the familiar algebraic notion: if \(X=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\), \(Y=\operatorname{Spec}(B)\), and \(\mathcal F=\widetilde M\), then flatness is controlled by the \(B\)-module \(M\) coming from \(B\to A\).

Lemma 1 With the notation above, \(\mathcal F\) is flat over \(Y\) if and only if \(M\) is flat as a \(B\)-module.


Proof. It is an easy commutative algebra exercise.


Corollary 1 If \(\pi:X\to Y\) is an affine morphism, and \(\mathcal F\) is a quasicoherent sheaf on \(X\), then \(\mathcal F\) is flat over \(Y\) if and only if \(\pi_*\mathcal F\) is flat over \(Y\).







Warningnonexample



The statement may fail even when \(\pi\) is quasi-compact and quasi-separated.
Consider the composite \[
\pi\colon \mathbb P^1_k\hookrightarrow \mathbb P^1_{k[x]} \to \operatorname{Spec}k[x],
\text{ and set }
\mathcal F=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1_k}(-1).
\] Then \(\mathcal F\) is a line bundle and hence flat over \(\mathbb P^1_{k}\).
On the other hand, the global section of \(\pi_*\mathcal F\) is \(H^0(\mathbf P^1_k,\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^1_k}(-1))=0\), which implies that \(\pi_*\mathcal F\) is not flat.



Definition 2 (flat morphism) A morphism \(\pi\colon X\to Y\) is flat at \(x\in X\) if the local ring \(\mathcal O_{X,x}\) is flat over \(\mathcal O_{Y,\pi(x)}\). It is flat if it is flat at every point, i.e. \(\mathcal O_X\) is flat over \(Y\).
Equivalently, by Lemma 1, \(\pi\colon X\to Y\) is flat if there exist affine open coverings \(X=\bigcup_i X_i\) and \(Y=\bigcup_i Y_i\) such that \(\pi(X_i)\subseteq Y_i\) for each \(i\), and \(A_i\) is flat over \(B_i\) whenever \(X_i=\operatorname{Spec}A_i\) and \(Y_i=\operatorname{Spec}B_i\).


Proposition 1 (flat morphisms form a reasonable class) Flat morphisms satisfy the following properties one expects from a geometric class of morphisms:

isomorphisms and open immersions are flat;
the composite \(\phi\circ\pi\colon X\to Z\) is flat whenever both \(\pi\) and \(\phi\) are flat;
flatness is preserved by base change: if \(\pi\colon X\to Y\) is flat and \(\psi\colon Y'\to Y\) is any morphism, then \(X\times_Y Y'\to Y'\) is flat;
flatness is local on both the source and the target.



Proof. The assersions 1 and 4 follow immediately by the definition. Assersion 2,3 follow from the corresponding properties for flat quasicoherent sheaves, see Lemma 2 and Lemma 3.


Lemma 2 Let \(\pi\colon X\to Y\) be a morphism, and let \(\mathcal F\) be a quasicoherent sheaf on \(X\) that is flat over \(Y\). Let \(\phi\colon Y\to Z\) be a flat morphism. Then \(\mathcal F\) is flat over \(Z\).


Proof. By definition, it suffices to check on stalks.


Lemma 3 Let \(X\to Y\) and \(Y'\to Y\) be morphisms. Let \(\mu\colon X'=X\times_Y Y'\to X\) be the projection, and \(\mathcal F\) a quasicoherent sheaf on \(X\) flat over \(Y\). Then \(\mu^*\mathcal F\) is flat over \(Y'\).


Proof. By definition, it suffices to check on stalks. Let \(x'\in X'\). Assume that \(x'\) maps to \(x\in X\), \(y'\in Y'\) and \(y\in Y\) respectively. Then \(\mathcal O_{X',x'}\cong (\mathcal O_{X,x}\otimes_{\mathcal O_{Y,y}} \mathcal O_{Y',y'})_{\mathfrak p}\) for some prime ideal \(\mathfrak p\). Then \[
(\mu^*\mathcal F)_{x'}\cong (\mathcal O_{X,x}\otimes_{\mathcal O_{Y,y}} \mathcal O_{Y',y'})_{\mathfrak p}\otimes_{\mathcal O_{X,x}}\mathcal F_x.
\] The rest is a commutative algebra exercise.

title: Flat Morphisms
text:
Criteria of flatness

Proposition 2 (Tor criterion) A \(B\)-module \(M\) is flat if and only if
\[
\operatorname{Tor}_1^B(M,N)=0
\]
for every \(B\)-module \(N\).


Proposition 3 (ideal criterion) A \(B\)-module \(M\) is flat if and only if, for every finitely generated ideal \(I\subseteq B\), the natural map
\[
I\otimes_B M\longrightarrow M
\]
is injective. The map sends \(a\otimes m\) to \(am\). Equivalently, we can only check \(N\) for finitely generated ideals of \(B\) in Proposition 2.


Proposition 4 Let \((B,\mathfrak n)\) be a local ring and \(M\) a finitely generated \(B\)-module. If \(\operatorname{Tor}(M,B/\mathfrak n)=0\), then \(M\) is free.


Proposition 5 (local criterion) Let \((B,\mathfrak n)\to (A,\mathfrak m)\) be a local morphism of Noetherian local rings, and \(M\) a finitely generated \(A\) module. Then \(M\) is \(B\)-flat if and only if \(\operatorname {Tor}^B_1(M,B/\mathfrak n)=0\).


Proposition 6 (slicing criterion for flatness) Let \((B,\mathfrak n)\to (A,\mathfrak m)\) be a local morphism of Noetherian local rings, \(M\) a finitely generated \(A\)-module, and \(t\in \mathfrak n\) a non-zerodivisor on \(B\). Then \(M\) is flat over \(B\) if and only if

\(t\) is not a zerodivisor on \(M\), and
\(M/tM\) is flat over \(B/(t)\).

title: Flat Morphisms
text:
Examples

Example 1 Let \(k\) be a field and consider
\[
\pi\colon\mathbb A_k^2\longrightarrow\mathbb A_k^1,
\qquad (x,y)\longmapsto xy.
\]
Algebraically, \(\pi\) is induced by
\[
B=k[t]\longrightarrow A=k[x,y],
\qquad t\longmapsto xy.
\]
The \(B\)-module \(A\) is torsion-free, hence flat because \(B=k[t]\) is a PID. For \(a\ne0\), the fiber \(xy=a\) is a smooth hyperbola, while the fiber over \(0\) is
\[
V(xy)=V(x)\cup V(y),
\]
the union of the two coordinate axes. Moreover, the inclusion \(V(xy)\hookrightarrow\mathbb A_k^2\) is a codimension-one regular embedding, since \(xy\) is a non-zero-divisor in \(k[x,y]\).







WarningFlat does not mean smooth



The special fiber in Example 1 is singular at the origin even though the family is flat. Flatness controls how fibers vary; it does not say that every fiber is nonsingular.

title: Étale Morphisms
text:
NoteSite



“An étale morphism is the analogue in algebraic geometry of a local isomorphism of manifolds in differential geometry, a covering of Riemann surfaces with no branch points in complex analysis, and an unramiﬁed extension in algebraic number theory.”–Milne.


Since the author, I, hasn’t learned flat morphisms and unramified morphisms seriously yet, but already has a basic understanding of the étale site and étale cohomology, which means that the author is familiar to some basic properties of étale morphisms and use it. Our main goal in this chapter is to understand the various equivalent definitions of étale morphisms and to get some intuition for what they are analog to. One of the purpose of this chapter is to figure out which property of étale morphisms comes from the flatness and which property comes from the unramifiedness. The author will try to understand the definition of étale morphisms in a more intuitive way, and then try to understand the properties of étale morphisms from the perspective of flatness and unramifiedness.
For a first pass, continue to Definitions.
For a more detailed discussion, see Flat Morphisms, The Sheaf of Differentials and Unramified Morphisms, and Smooth Morphisms …(TBA)

title: Smooth Morphisms
text: A smooth morphism is the relative version of a nonsingular variety. Roughly, its fibers are smooth and fit together uniformly over the base.

title: Smooth Morphisms
text:
Defitions

Definition 1 (standard smooth morphism) The projection
\[
\operatorname{Spec}(R[x_1,\cdot, \cdot, x_{n+r}]/(f_1,\cdot, f_r)) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Spec}(R)
\]
is called the standard smooth morphism of relative dimension \(n\) if the determinant of the matrix
\[
\left(\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r}
\]
is invertible in the ring \(R[x_1,\cdot, \cdot, x_{n+r}]/(f_1,\cdot, f_r)\).


Remark 1. The fibers of this morphism are smooth varieties of dimension \(n\) by the Jacobian criterion. The condition on the determinant is a relative version of the Jacobian criterion.


Definition 2 (smooth morphism) A morphism \(f\colon X\to Y\) between schemes is smooth of relative dimension \(n\) if there exist open coverings \(\{U_i\}\) of \(X\) and \(\{V_i\}\) of \(Y\) such that \(f(U_i)\subseteq V_i\) and for each \(i\), the restriction \(f|_{U_i}\colon U_i\to V_i\) is a standard smooth morphism of relative dimension \(n\).


Remark 2. There are several equivalent variants of the definition of a standard smooth morphism that lead to the same notion of a smooth morphism.

We may allow a morphism which factors as \[
U \hookrightarrow
\operatorname{Spec}\bigl(R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+r}]/(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\bigr)
\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Spec}(R),
\] where the first morphism is an open immersion and the second morphism is standard smooth in the sense above.
We may replace the prescribed square Jacobian matrix by the full Jacobian matrix \[
\left(\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}\right)_
{\substack{1\leq i\leq r\\1\leq j\leq n+r}},
\] and require that some \(r\times r\) minor be invertible.

These variants give the same notion of a smooth morphism.


Definition 3 (smooth variety) A variety \(X\) over a field \(k\) is smooth if the structure morphism \(X\to \operatorname{Spec}(k)\) is smooth.







Tip



Such definition for smooth variety is a little bit indirect, but it is convenient for our discussion since we will not spend much time on smooth varieties.

title: Smooth Morphisms
text:
Basic properties

Proposition 1 If \(f\colon X\to Y\) and \(g\colon Y\to Z\) are smooth morphisms of relative dimension \(n\) and \(m\) respectively, then the composition \(g\circ f\colon X\to Z\) is also smooth of relative dimension \(n+m\).


Proof. This is a local property, so we can assume that \(f\) and \(g\) are standard smooth morphisms of relative dimension \(n\) and \(m\) respectively. Then, by the chain rule, the corresponding Jacobian matrix of the composition \(g\circ f\) is a block-upper-triangular matrix with the Jacobian matrices of \(f\) and \(g\) on the diagonal. Therefore, the determinant of the corresponding square matrix of \(g\circ f\) is the product of determinants of the square matrices of \(f\) and \(g\), which are both invertible. So \(g\circ f\) is a standard smooth morphism of relative dimension \(n+m\).


Relation to differentials
We recall the definition and properties of the sheaf of differentials in The Sheaf of Differentials and Unramified Morphisms. The sheaf of differentials can be used to characterize smooth morphisms and smooth varieties.

Proposition 2 A variety \(X\) over \(k\) is smooth if and only if the sheaf of differentials \(\Omega_{X/k}\) is locally free of rank \(\dim(X)\).


Proof. When \(\Omega_{X/k}\) is locally free of rank \(\dim(X)\), we know that the Jacobian matrix has full rank at every point, which implies that \(X\) is smooth. Conversely, assume \(X\) is smooth. Then, by the relation between smoothness and regualrness, one can show that \(X\) is reduced. Since \(X\) is of finite type, the sheaf of differentials \(\Omega_{X/k}\) is of finite type. By the relation between the cotangent space and the fibre of the sheaf of differentials, we have \(\dim_{k(x)}(\Omega_{X/k}\otimes k(x))=\dim(X)\) for all closed points \(x\in X\). Therefore, we conclude that \(\Omega_{X/k}\) is locally free of rank \(\dim(X)\).







CautionCaution



It is not easy to show that a smooth variety is reduced. The proof is not included here, but it can be found in the textbook “The Rising Sea”. And the last statement in the proof above is a corollary of Nakayama’s lemma, which is a fundamental result in alegbraic geometry, and both reducedness, finiteness and the constantness of the dimension of fibre matter. See 14.3.J in “The Rising Sea” for details.



Proposition 3 Let \(f\colon X\to Y\) and \(g\colon Y\to Z\) be morphisms of schemes. If \(f\) and \(g\) are smooth, then the transitive exact sequence is also exact on the left, which means that the sequence \[
0\to f^*\Omega_{Y/Z}\to \Omega_{X/Z}\to \Omega_{X/Y}\to 0
\]
is exact.


Proof. This is a local property, so we can assume that \(f\) and \(g\) are standard smooth morphisms of relative dimension \(n\) and \(m\) respectively. In The Sheaf of Differentials and Unramified Morphisms, we know the module of differentials is the cokernel of the Jacobian matrix. The injectivity of the left follows from the fact that the Jacobian matrix of \(g\circ f\) is a block-upper-triangular matrix with the Jacobian matrices of \(f\) and \(g\) on the diagonal.

In the following, we will discuss the conormal exact sequence.

Theorem 1 Let \(i:X\hookrightarrow Y\) be a closed immersion of smooth varieties over a field \(k\), with ideal sheaf \(\mathcal I\). Then the conormal sheaf \[
\mathcal N^\vee_{X/Y}:=\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2
\] is locally free, and the conormal sequence is a locally split short exact sequence \[
0\longrightarrow \mathcal N^\vee_{X/Y}
\xrightarrow{\delta}i^*\Omega_{Y/k}
\longrightarrow\Omega_{X/k}
\longrightarrow 0,
\] where \(\delta(\overline f)=df|_X\).
Dualizing gives the normal exact sequence \[
0\longrightarrow\mathcal T_{X/k}
\longrightarrow i^*\mathcal T_{Y/k}
\longrightarrow\mathcal N_{X/Y}
\longrightarrow 0,
\] where \(\mathcal N_{X/Y}:=(\mathcal N^\vee_{X/Y})^\vee\).


Proof. Differentials and the conormal sheaf commute with field extension, while exactness and finite local freeness descend under faithfully flat base change. We may therefore assume that \(k\) is algebraically closed.
Since \(X\) and \(Y\) are smooth over \(k\), they are regular, and the closed immersion \(i\) is a regular immersion. Thus \(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2\) is locally free of rank equal to the codimension of \(X\) in \(Y\).
The conormal sequence is always right exact: \[
\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2
\xrightarrow{\delta}i^*\Omega_{Y/k}
\longrightarrow\Omega_{X/k}
\longrightarrow 0.
\] Set \(\mathcal K=\ker\delta\). Since \(\mathcal K\) is a subsheaf of the locally free sheaf \(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2\), we have \[
\operatorname{Ass}(\mathcal K)
\subseteq\operatorname{Ass}(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2)
\subseteq\operatorname{Ass}(\mathcal O_X).
\] As \(X\) is reduced, its associated points are precisely the generic points of its irreducible components. Moreover, every nonzero coherent sheaf has an associated point. Hence it suffices to show that \(\mathcal K_\eta=0\) at every generic point \(\eta\) of \(X\).
Fix such a point \(\eta\), and work locally where \(X\) and \(Y\) have dimensions \(m\) and \(n\), respectively. Since \(X\) is reduced, \(\mathcal O_{X,\eta}=\kappa(\eta)\) is a field. Taking stalks gives a right-exact sequence of vector spaces \[
(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2)_\eta
\xrightarrow{\delta_\eta}(i^*\Omega_{Y/k})_\eta
\longrightarrow(\Omega_{X/k})_\eta
\longrightarrow 0.
\] The dimensions of these three vector spaces are \(n-m\), \(n\), and \(m\), respectively. Right exactness therefore gives \[
\dim_{\kappa(\eta)}\operatorname{im}\delta_\eta=n-m
=\dim_{\kappa(\eta)}(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2)_\eta.
\] Thus \(\delta_\eta\) is injective. It follows that \(\mathcal K=0\), proving left exactness.
Since \(\Omega_{X/k}\) is locally free, the resulting short exact sequence splits locally. Dualizing a locally split short exact sequence preserves exactness, giving the normal sequence.


Corollary 1 Let \(Y\) be a smooth variety over a field \(k\), and let \(q\in Y\) be a closed point such that \(\kappa(q)/k\) is separable. Write \(\mathfrak m_q\) for the maximal ideal of \(\mathcal O_{Y,q}\). Then the map \[
\mathfrak m_q/\mathfrak m_q^2
\xrightarrow{\sim}
\Omega_{Y/k}\otimes_{\mathcal O_Y}\kappa(q),
\qquad
\overline f\longmapsto df\otimes 1,
\] is a canonical isomorphism.


Proof. The extension \(\kappa(q)/k\) is finite separable, so \(\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(q)\) is smooth over \(k\) and \(\Omega_{\kappa(q)/k}=0\). Applying the preceding theorem to the closed immersion \(\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(q)\hookrightarrow Y\) gives \[
0\longrightarrow\mathfrak m_q/\mathfrak m_q^2
\longrightarrow\Omega_{Y/k}\otimes_{\mathcal O_Y}\kappa(q)
\longrightarrow\Omega_{\kappa(q)/k}
\longrightarrow 0.
\] The last term vanishes, proving the first assertion.







Note



The separability hypothesis is automatic when \(k\) is perfect, in particular when \(\operatorname{char}k=0\) or \(k\) is finite. And the statement still holds when we do not require the smoothness of \(Y\).

title: The Sheaf of Differentials and Unramified Morphisms
text: To study unramified morphisms, we need to understand the sheaf of differentials first.
crumbs: The Sheaf of Differentials and Unramified Morphisms

title: The Sheaf of Differentials and Unramified Morphisms
section: Definition of the sheaf of differentials
text:
Definition of the sheaf of differentials
For schemes \(X\) over \(Y\), there is a quasicoherent sheaf, \(\Omega_{X/Y}\), on \(X\). We call it the sheaf of differentials.

Definition 1 (sheaf of differentials) The sheaf \(\Omega_{X/Y}\) is globally defined as the quotient \(\mathscr I/\mathscr I^2\), where the ideal sheaf \(\mathscr I\) is the sheaf of ideals defining the diagonal embedding \(X\to X\times_Y X\). One can check that \(\Omega_{X/Y}\) is indeed a sheaf on \(X\). We define a map \(d\colon \mathscr O_X\to \Omega_{X/Y}\) by \(d(f)=\operatorname{pr}_1^*f-\operatorname{pr}_2^*f\) for \(f\in \mathscr O_X\).


Proposition 1 Affine locally, if \(X=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) and \(Y=\operatorname{Spec}(B)\), then \(\Omega_{X/Y}\) is the sheaf associated to the \(A\)-module \(\Omega_{A/B}\), which is generated by symbols \(da\) for \(a\in A\) subject to the relations:

\(d(a+a')=da+da'\) for all \(a,a'\in A\),
\(d(aa')=a\,da'+a'\,da\) for all \(a,a'\in A\), and
\(db=0\) for all \(b\in B\).



Proof. By definition, \(\Omega_{X/Y}\) is the sheaf associated to the \(A\)-module \(I/I^2\), where \(I\) is the kernel of the morphism \(A\otimes_B A\to A\). It is generated by elements of the form \(a\otimes 1-1\otimes a\) for \(a\in A\). One can check that the map \(\Omega_{A/B}\longrightarrow I/I^2\) given by \(da\mapsto a\otimes 1-1\otimes a\) is an isomorphism of \(A\)-modules.


Remark 1 (the universal property). The module \(\Omega_{A/B}\) is universal for \(B\)-derivations from \(A\) to an \(A\)-module \(M\). We skip the proof here, but one can find it in any standard textbook on algebraic geometry.
crumbs: The Sheaf of Differentials and Unramified Morphisms

title: The Sheaf of Differentials and Unramified Morphisms
text:
Basic properties of \(\Omega_{X/Y}\)
There are two standard exact sequences of sheaves of differentials. The first one is the transitivity sequence: for morphisms \(f:X\to Y\) and \(g:Y\to Z\), there is an exact sequence \[
f^*\Omega_{Y/Z}\longrightarrow \Omega_{X/Z}\longrightarrow \Omega_{X/Y}\longrightarrow 0.
\]
The second one is the conormal sequence: for a closed immersion \(i:X\hookrightarrow Y\) with ideal sheaf \(\mathscr I\), there is an exact sequence \[
\mathscr I/\mathscr I^2\longrightarrow i^*\Omega_{Y/Z}\longrightarrow \Omega_{X/Z}\longrightarrow 0.
\]






NoteConormal sheaf



We call \(\mathscr I/\mathscr I^2\) the conormal sheaf of \(X\) in \(Y\). It is a vector bundle on \(X\) if \(i:X\hookrightarrow Y\) is a regular immersion.


The sheaf of differentials \(\Omega_{X/Y}\) is compatible with base change: for a cartesian diagram \[
\begin{array}{ccc}
X' & \xrightarrow{\mu} & X \\
\downarrow & {\square}\,& \downarrow \\
Y' & \longrightarrow & Y
\end{array}
\] we have a canonical isomorphism \[
\Omega_{X'/Y'}\cong \mu^*\Omega_{X/Y}.
\]
All these properties can be done by using Proposition 1 and the corresponding properties of \(\Omega_{A/B}\).






TipHint



For the two exact sequences, one can check the right one is indeed the cokernel. For the base change property, one can use the universal property of \(\Omega_{A/B}\).


Here is a property for \(\Omega_{A/B}\). For a localization \(S^{-1}A\) of \(A\), we have a canonical isomorphism \[
\Omega_{S^{-1}A/B}\cong S^{-1}\Omega_{A/B}.
\] One can check this using the universal properties of the module of differentials and localization, or using the explicit description of \(\Omega_{A/B}\) in Proposition 1.
There is a proposition characterizing the sheaf of differntials for the fibre product.

Proposition 2 Let \(\alpha:X\to Z\) and \(\beta:Y\to Z\) be morphisms of schemes, and let \(W=X\times_ZY\), with projections \(p:W\to X\) and \(q:W\to Y\). There is a canonical isomorphism \[
p^*\Omega_{X/Z}\oplus q^*\Omega_{Y/Z}
\xrightarrow{\sim}\Omega_{W/Z},
\] given by the sum of the natural maps on differentials.


Proof. Write \[
u:p^*\Omega_{X/Z}\longrightarrow\Omega_{W/Z},
\qquad
v:q^*\Omega_{Y/Z}\longrightarrow\Omega_{W/Z}
\] for the natural maps. By transitivity and base change for differentials, we have an exact sequence \[
p^*\Omega_{X/Z}\xrightarrow{u}\Omega_{W/Z}
\xrightarrow{s}q^*\Omega_{Y/Z}\longrightarrow 0,
\] where we identify \(\Omega_{W/X}\cong q^*\Omega_{Y/Z}\). Naturality gives \(s\circ v=\operatorname{id}\).
Similarly, the natural quotient map \[
\Omega_{W/Z}\longrightarrow\Omega_{W/Y}
\cong p^*\Omega_{X/Z}
\] is a left inverse to \(u\), so \(u\) is injective. Thus the sequence above is short exact and split by \(v\). Consequently, \[
u\oplus v:
p^*\Omega_{X/Z}\oplus q^*\Omega_{Y/Z}
\xrightarrow{\sim}\Omega_{W/Z}
\] is the desired canonical isomorphism.
crumbs: The Sheaf of Differentials and Unramified Morphisms

title: The Sheaf of Differentials and Unramified Morphisms
text:
Easy calculations of some \(\Omega_{A/B}\)

A useful lemma

Lemma 1 Let \(B\) be a ring and \(A=B[x_1,x_2, \cdots]/(r_1, r_2, \cdots)\) be the ring over \(B\). Then \(\Omega_{A/B}\) is a free \(A\)-module generated by \(dx_1, dx_2, \cdots\) modulo the relations \(dr_1, dr_2, \cdots\).


Proof. For the convenience of the proof, we assume that \(A=B[x_1, x_2, \cdots]\). The general case can be reduced to this case by using the transitivity sequence. Let \(M=\oplus_i A\,e_i\) be the free \(A\)-module generated by \(e_1, e_2, \cdots\). We define a map \(\phi\colon M\to \Omega_{A/B}\) by sending \(e_i\) to \(dx_i\) in \(\Omega_{A/B}\). One can check that \(\phi\) is surjective. To show that \(\phi\) is injective, we construct an inverse map \(\psi\colon \Omega_{A/B}\to M\). For any \(a\in A\), we can write it as a polynomial in \(x_1, x_2, \cdots,x_n\). We define \(\psi(da)\) to be the formal differential of this polynomial. One can check that \(\psi\) is well-defined and is indeed the inverse of \(\phi\).



Differentials for field extensions

Lemma 2 Let \(L/K\) be a separable field extension. Then \(\Omega_{L/K}=0\).


Proof. For any \(\alpha\in L\), there exists a polynomial \(f\in K[x]\) such that \(f(\alpha)=0\) and \(f'(\alpha)\neq 0\). Then \(f'(\alpha)d\alpha=df(\alpha)=0\), which implies \(d\alpha=0\). Since \(\Omega_{L/K}\) is generated by \(d\alpha\) for \(\alpha\in L\), we have \(\Omega_{L/K}=0\).


Lemma 3 Let \(L/K\) be a purely inseparable field extension. Then \(\Omega_{L/K}\neq 0\).


Proof. Assume \(\text{char}(K)=p>0\). By the transitivity sequence and the structure of purely inseparable extensions, we may assume \(L=K[x]/(x^p-a)\) for some \(a\in K\). By Lemma 1, we have \(\Omega_{L/K}\cong L\,dx/(px^{p-1}\,dx)=L\,dx\neq 0\).


Lemma 4 If \(L/K\) is separably genrated by \(t_1,\cdots,t_n\in K\), then \(\Omega_{L/K}\) is a free \(L\)-module generated by \(dt_1,\cdots, dt_n\).


Proof. By Lemma 1 and localization, we have \[\Omega_{K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)/K}\cong K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)\,dt_1\oplus\cdots\oplus K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)\,dt_n.\]
By Lemma 2, we have \(\Omega_{L/K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)}=0\), which implies \(\Omega_{L/K}\cong L\,dt_1+\cdots+ L\,dt_n\) by the transitivity sequence. It remains to show that \(dt_1,\cdots, dt_n\) are linearly independent over \(L\). We will prove this by showing that there exist \(K\) derivations \(d_i\) such that \(d_i(t_j)=\delta_{ij}\). For any \(i\), we can extend the derivation \(\frac{\partial}{\partial t_i}\) on \(K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)\) to a derivation \(d_i\) on \(L\) by using the fact that \(L/K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)\) is separable. To be precise, if \(\alpha\in L\) is algebraic over \(K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)\), then there exists a polynomial \(f\in K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)[x]\) such that \(f(\alpha)=0\) and \(f'(\alpha)\neq 0\). We can define \(d_i(\alpha)\) to be the unique solution of the equation \(f'(\alpha)d_i(\alpha)+d_i(f)(\alpha)=0\). One can check that \(d_i\) is indeed a derivation on \(L\) and \(d_i(t_j)=\delta_{ij}\).



Differentials for normalization

Example 1 (differentials for the normalization of a curve with a node) Let \[
A=k[x,y]/(y^2-x^2(x+1)),\quad B=k[t],\quad \operatorname{char} k\neq 2,
\] with \(x\mapsto t^2-1\) and \(y\mapsto t(t^2-1)\). The induced map on differentials is \[
dx\longmapsto 2t\,dt,\qquad
dy\longmapsto (3t^2-1)\,dt.
\] Consequently, \[
\Omega_{B/A}
\cong \frac{k[t]}{(2t,3t^2-1)}\,dt=0,
\] since \(\operatorname{char}k\neq 2\) and \[
1=\frac{3}{2}t(2t)-(3t^2-1).
\] Hence the normalization morphism is unramified everywhere, including at \(t=\pm1\), the two points lying over the node.


Example 2 (differentials for the normalization of a curve with a cusp) Let \[
A=k[x,y]/(y^2-x^3),\qquad B=k[t],
\] with normalization map \(x\mapsto t^2\) and \(y\mapsto t^3\). The induced map on differentials is \[
dx\longmapsto 2t\,dt,\qquad
dy\longmapsto 3t^2\,dt.
\] Therefore \[
\Omega_{B/A}
\cong \frac{k[t]}{(2t,3t^2)}\,dt
\cong
\begin{cases}
(k[t]/(t))\,dt, & \operatorname{char}k\neq 2,\\
(k[t]/(t^2))\,dt, & \operatorname{char}k=2.
\end{cases}
\] Thus the normalization morphism is unramified away from \(t=0\), but is not unramified at the point lying over the cusp.



Relation to the cotangent space

Proposition 3 Let \(X\) be a scheme over \(k\) and \(x\in X\) be a closed point with residue field \(\kappa (x)\) separable over \(k\). Then the cotangent space of \(X\) at \(x\) is isomorphic to \(\Omega_{X/k}\otimes \kappa(x)\).


Proof. Apply the conormal sequence to the closed immersion \(\operatorname{Spec}(k(x))\hookrightarrow X\), we have a map \(\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2 \rightarrow \Omega_{X/k}\otimes \kappa(x)\), where \(\mathfrak m_x\) is the maximal ideal of \(\mathcal O_{X,x}\). We will show this surjection is actually a bijection. For convenience, let \(A=\mathcal O_{X,x}\) ,\(k'=\kappa(x)\) and \(\mathfrak m=\mathfrak m_x\). Since the module of differentials is compatible with localization, it suffices to show that the map \(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2 \rightarrow \Omega_{A/k}\otimes k'\) is a bijection. By Yoneda lemma, it suffices to show that for any \(k'\)-module \(M\), the map \[
\operatorname{Hom}_{k'}(\Omega_{A/k}\otimes k', M)\to \operatorname{Hom}_{k'}(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2, M)
\]
is a bijection. By the universal property of \(\Omega_{A/k}\), we have a bijection \(\operatorname{Hom}_{A}(\Omega_{A/k}, M)\cong \operatorname{Der}_k(A,M)\). By Lemma 2, we have \(\operatorname{Der}_k(k',M)=0\), which means that \[\operatorname{Der}_k(A,M)=\operatorname{Der}_{k'}(A,M)\cong \operatorname{Der}_{k'}(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2,M).\]
One checks that this is just the map defined above, and the last isomorphism will be shown when we discuss formally étale.







TipVariety case



In case when \(X\) and \(Y\) are varieties and \(x\) is a \(k\)-point, by Lemma 1, we could deduce that \(\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2\) and \(\Omega_{X/k}\otimes k\) both come from the cokernel of the Jacobian matrix. So they are isomorphic.

title: The Sheaf of Differentials and Unramified Morphisms
text:
Unramified morphisms

Definition 2 (unramified morphism) A morphism \(\pi\colon X\to Y\) between schemes is unramified if it is locally of finite type and \(\Omega_{X/Y}=0\).

By the transitivity sequence, unramified morphisms are stable under composition. By the base change property, unramified morphisms are stable under base change. One checks that unramified morphisms are also local on the target, so they are ``reasonable’’ in the sense of the textbook the rising sea.

Proposition 4 Let \(\pi:X\to Y\) be a morphism locally of finite type, then the locus in \(X\) where \(\pi\) is unramified is open.


Proof. The locus is the complement of \(\operatorname {supp}(\Omega_{X/Y})\), which is naturally open.


Examples
By the above calculation of \(\Omega_{A/B}\), we have the following corollaries.

Corollary 1 If \(L/K\) is a field extension of finite type, then \(\operatorname{Spec}(L) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Spec}(K)\) is unramified if and only if \(L/K\) is a finite separable extension.


Proof. By Lemma 2, it suffices to show that if \(\operatorname{Spec}(L) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Spec}(K)\) is unramified then \(L/K\) is a finite separable extension.
If \(L/K\) is inseparable, then \(\Omega_{L/K}\neq 0\) by the transitive exact sequence and Lemma 3. Thus, \(L/K\) is separable. If \(L/K\) is trancendental, then \(\Omega_{L/K}\neq 0\) by Lemma 4. Therefore, the extension \(L/K\) must be algebraic separable, which impies that \(L/K\) is finite since it is algebraic and of finite type.


Example 3 (coincidence in number theory) Let \(\phi:(A,\mathfrak m)\to (B,\mathfrak n)\) is a local morphism of finite type between local rings. Then \(\phi\) is unramifed if and only if \(B/\phi(\mathfrak m)B\) is a finite separable extension of \(A/\mathfrak m\).


Proof. It is a immediate consequence of Proposition 6.



Criterions of unramifiedness

Proposition 5 Let \(\pi:X\to Y\) and \(\rho:Y\to Z\) be morphisms locally of finite type, and let \(\tau=\rho\circ\pi\). If \(\tau\) is unramified, then \(\pi\) is unramified.


Proof. The transitivity sequence gives a surjection \[
\Omega_{X/Z}\longrightarrow
\Omega_{X/Y}\longrightarrow 0.
\] Since \(\tau:X\to Z\) is unramified, we have \(\Omega_{X/Z}=0\). Therefore \(\Omega_{X/Y}=0\). As \(\pi\) is locally of finite type, it follows that \(\pi\) is unramified.


Proposition 6 Let \(\pi:X\to Y\) be a morphism locally of finite type. Then the following are equivalent.

\(\pi\) is unramifed,
for each point \(y\in Y\), \(\pi^{-1}(y)\) is the disjoint union of schemes of the form \(\operatorname {Spec} K\) where \(K\) is a finite separable extension of \(\kappa(y)\), and
for each geometric point \(\bar y\in Y\), \(\pi^{-1}(\bar y)\) is the disjoint union of copies of \(\bar y\).



Proof. Assersion 1 implies 2 and 3 by Corollary 1 and base change. Assersion 2 (resp. 3) implies that \(\Omega_{X/Y}|_y=0\) (resp. \(\Omega_{X/Y}|_{\bar y}=0\)). Since \(\Omega_{X/Y}\) is of finte type, assersion 1 follows from the fact that if a quasicoherent sheaf \(\mathcal F\) of finite type on \(Y\) and \(\mathcal F|_y=0\) for all \(y\in Y\), then \(\mathcal F=0\). Note that \(\mathcal F|_y=0\) implies that \(\mathcal F_y=0\) by Nakayama’s lemma.


Proposition 7 Let \(\pi:X\to Y\) be a morphism between finite type schemes over an algebraically closed field \(k\). Then \(\pi\) is unramified if and only if \(\pi\) is injective on tangent vectors at closed points.


Proof. For any closed point \(x\in X\), let \(y\) be its image in \(Y\), then \(y\) is also a closed point \(Y\). By the transitive sequence, we have \[
\pi^*\Omega_{Y/k}\to\Omega_{X/k}\to\Omega_{X/Y}\to 0.
\]
Pullback to \(x=\operatorname{Spec}k\), we have \[
\Omega_{Y/k}|_y\to\Omega_{X/k}|_x\to\Omega_{X/Y}|_x\to 0.
\]
By Proposition 3 and the assumption, we know that \(\Omega_{Y/k}|_y\to\Omega_{X/k}|_x\) is the morphism between the corresponding cotangent spaces and hence surjective. Therfore, \(\Omega_{X/Y}|_x=0\), which mimplies that \(\pi\) is unramified at \(x\). Since the closed points are dense in \(X\), \(\pi\) is unramifed by Proposition 4.


Proposition 8 Let \(\pi:X\to Y\) be a morphism locally of finite type. Then \(\pi\colon X\to Y\) is unramified when its diagonal morphism \(X\to X\times_Y X\) is an open immersion.


Proof. We first record a lemma. Let \(i:Z\hookrightarrow W\) be a closed immersion whose ideal sheaf \(\mathcal I\) is of finite type. If \(\mathcal I=\mathcal I^2\), then \(i\) is also an open immersion.
Indeed, it is enough to work on an affine open subset \(\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq W\). Let \(I\subseteq A\) be the corresponding finitely generated ideal. For every prime ideal \(\mathfrak p\) containing \(I\), we have \[
I_{\mathfrak p}=I_{\mathfrak p}^2\subseteq \mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}I_{\mathfrak p}.
\] Since \(I_{\mathfrak p}\) is finitely generated, Nakayama’s lemma gives \(I_{\mathfrak p}=0\). Consequently, \[
V(I)\cap\operatorname{Supp}(I)=\varnothing.
\] Conversely, if \(\mathfrak p\notin V(I)\), then \(I_{\mathfrak p}=A_{\mathfrak p}\neq0\), so \(\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Supp}(I)\). Hence \[
V(I)=\operatorname{Spec}A\setminus\operatorname{Supp}(I).
\] Because \(I\) is finitely generated, \(\operatorname{Supp}(I)\) is closed. Thus \(V(I)\) is open, proving the lemma.
We now apply the lemma to the diagonal. Since \(\pi\) is locally of finite type, \(\Delta_\pi\) is locally of finite presentation. To see this locally, write \[
B\longrightarrow A=B[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/J.
\] The multiplication map \(A\otimes_BA\longrightarrow A\) has kernel generated by the finitely many elements \[
x_i\otimes1-1\otimes x_i,\qquad 1\leq i\leq n.
\] Thus the diagonal is, locally on its source and target, a closed immersion defined by an ideal sheaf \(\mathcal I\) of finite type.
Suppose first that \(\pi\) is unramified. Then \(\Omega_{X/Y}=0\). Since \(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2\cong\Omega_{X/Y}\), it follows that \(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2=0\), and hence \(\mathcal I=\mathcal I^2\). The lemma therefore shows, locally around every point of \(\Delta_\pi(X)\), that the diagonal is an open immersion. Hence \(\Delta_\pi\) is an open immersion.
Conversely, suppose that \(\Delta_\pi\) is an open immersion. An open immersion has zero conormal sheaf, so \(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2=0\), which implies that \(\Omega_{X/Y}=0\). Since \(\pi\) is locally of finite type, this is precisely the condition that \(\pi\) be unramified.


Corollary 2 Let \(\mathcal P\) be a class of morphisms stable under base change and restriction to open subschemes of the source. Let \(\pi:X\to Y\) and \(\rho:Y\to Z\) be morphisms, and set \(\tau=\rho\circ\pi\). If \(\rho\) is unramified and \(\tau\) belongs to \(\mathcal P\), then \(\pi\) belongs to \(\mathcal P\).
In particular, if \(\tau\) is smooth of relative dimension \(n\) (resp. étale), then so is \(\pi\).


Proof. Factor \(\pi\) as \[
X\xrightarrow{\Gamma_\pi}X\times_ZY
\xrightarrow{\operatorname{pr}_2}Y,
\qquad
\Gamma_\pi=(\operatorname{id}_X,\pi).
\] The square \[
\begin{array}{ccc}
X & \xrightarrow{\Gamma_\pi} & X\times_ZY\\
{\scriptstyle\pi}\downarrow &&
\downarrow{\scriptstyle(\pi\circ\operatorname{pr}_1,\operatorname{pr}_2)}\\
Y & \xrightarrow{\Delta_\rho} & Y\times_ZY
\end{array}
\] is Cartesian. Since \(\rho\) is unramified, \(\Delta_\rho\) is an open immersion, and hence so is \(\Gamma_\pi\).
Moreover, \(\operatorname{pr}_2\) is the base change of \(\tau\) along \(\rho\), so it belongs to \(\mathcal P\). Thus \(\pi=\operatorname{pr}_2\circ\Gamma_\pi\) belongs to \(\mathcal P\) by stability under restriction to open subschemes of the source.
